h1: How to Avoid US Visa Appointment Scams, and What Happens to the Applicant When One Works
deck: The money is the smaller loss. In the cases that end worst the applicant loses the appointment, the scheduling account and the fee as well, and the intermediary who caused it is untouched.

headline: 2,000 appointments

coverSpec.title: When an intermediary breaks the scheduling rules, it is the applicant's appointment and account that are cancelled
coverSpec.desc: In March 2025 the US Mission in India cancelled about 2,000 visa appointments booked by automated means and suspended the scheduling privileges of the accounts involved. The applicants lost the appointment, the account and the money. The intermediaries who took the fee were not the ones sanctioned. The live 2026 scam patterns are advance-fee slot sales, fake demands for the $250 visa integrity fee, look-alike scheduling domains, and offers to sell the $750 expedite at posts where the pilot does not operate.

faq.q: What is the most common US visa appointment scam?
faq.a: Advance-fee slot selling. Someone in a messaging group offers an earlier interview date for a fee, shows screenshots of appointments as proof, takes payment, and either disappears or comes back asking for more. Reported cases in India describe applicants paying, receiving a fabricated confirmation, being asked for a second payment, and then being locked out of their own scheduling account.

faq.q: Can anyone reserve a US visa appointment slot for me before I apply?
faq.a: No. An appointment is created inside a scheduling account tied to your own DS-160 confirmation number and your own paid MRV fee receipt. Nobody can hold, reserve or pre-book a slot that then gets transferred to you, because there is nothing to transfer. Any offer of a slot before you have an account, a DS-160 and a paid fee is describing something that does not exist.

faq.q: What happens if my appointment was booked using automated tools?
faq.a: You can lose it. In March 2025 the US Mission in India cancelled roughly 2,000 appointments it identified as booked by automated means and suspended the scheduling privileges of the accounts involved. The sanction fell on the applicants' accounts, not on the intermediaries who took the money. That is the part worth understanding before paying anyone who is vague about method.

faq.q: Should I give a visa service my scheduling portal login?
faq.a: Treat it as a serious decision and never one you make in a chat window. Whoever holds your login can change your appointment, change your contact details or lock you out, and reported cases include exactly that. If a service does need account access to do its work, the questions to ask are what it collects, where it is held, how long it is kept and how you have it deleted, and the answers should be in published policies you can read before you pay.

faq.q: Someone is asking me to pay the $250 visa integrity fee. Is that real?
faq.a: The fee itself is real. A demand arriving by message, email or from an agent is not. The visa integrity fee is charged by the US government at the point your visa is issued, through your own consular process, and it is never collected by an intermediary or paid to a personal account. Because collection has rolled out unevenly across posts, a fake demand is unusually believable right now, which is exactly why it is being used.

faq.q: Can I get an earlier appointment by paying $750?
faq.a: Only at a participating mission. The State Department's expedited appointment pilot covers Mission Mexico and Mission Canada as of 19 August 2026, it is B-1/B-2 only, and the fee is paid to the US government inside your own scheduling account. Anyone selling a $750 expedite for a post that is not on the participating list is selling something that does not exist there, and there will be no fee to refund and no receipt to dispute.

faq.q: I have already paid a scammer. What can I do?
faq.a: Act on the account first and the money second. Change your scheduling account password and email, and check whether your appointment and contact details have been altered. Contact the official scheduling support channel for your country and tell them what happened. Report the fraud to your local police and to the US embassy or consulate that will adjudicate your application. Then raise it with your bank or payment provider, understanding that transfers to personal accounts are rarely recoverable.

cta.heading: The checks in this article apply to us too
cta.body: We are a paid service in a category full of fraud, so it would be strange to publish a scam guide and exempt ourselves from it. Everything you would use to check us is published before you pay: a named founder, real support channels, terms, a privacy policy and a refund policy, a price stated up front, and a written statement that nobody can promise you a date. Run the red flags below against us. If anything does not hold up, tell us and we will fix it.
